title: A stronger euro-area recovery could coexist with skill shortages and high unemployment
summary: Otmar Issing regarded the euro-area upswing as an opportunity to cut unemployment, with an important qualification for anyone trading the policy path. Stronger output did not in itself call for tighter money. What mattered was whether the economy could sustain the growth without inflation. Output had accelerated in the second half of 1999 and leading indicators pointed to continued strength. Most of the external forecasts he discussed put real GDP growth near 3% in both 2000 and 2001. These were forecasts from private and international institutions, not an ECB commitment, an estimate of potential growth or a measurement of news relative to market pricing (section 3).

His caution about capacity reflected the coexistence of considerable aggregate slack and local bottlenecks. Some 12.6 million people were seeking work, almost 10% of the workforce even before allowing for people who had stopped searching. Yet there were already reports of skilled-labour shortages in some member states. A vacancy that requires particular skills or is located far from an available worker can put upward pressure on wages despite high area-wide unemployment. The speech supplied no estimate of how many vacancies fell in that category. Nor did Issing accept that information technology had already lifted Europe onto a permanently higher, less inflationary growth path. He treated that proposition as contested even for the United States. In Europe, the accompanying flexibility of labour and product markets still had to be demonstrated.

The distinction was important because the new currency could improve financial conditions well before potential output improved. By removing volatility between member currencies, monetary union eliminated conversion costs and made prices easier to compare. Deeper markets could reduce liquidity premia. Credible disinflation could also reduce the compensation investors required for inflation uncertainty in long-term borrowing. Issing referred to the November ECB Monthly Bulletin’s finding that the fall in long real rates had been largest in member countries that entered the 1990s with the highest inflation. He interpreted this as evidence of lower risk premia and better investment financing conditions. It was a cross-country comparison during a period of convergence. The speech provided no decomposition into expected short rates, inflation risk, sovereign credit or liquidity. A lower financing cost is an incentive to invest, with no guarantee about the productivity or timing of the investment (sections 1 and 3).

Issing described the ECB’s reaction function in terms of two sources of evidence. The then-operative definition of price stability was a year-on-year increase in area-wide HICP below 2% over the medium term. Under the monetary pillar, 4.5% annual M3 growth was a reference value compatible with medium-term conditions. It did not impose a calendar-year cap or require a particular rate move after a monthly overshoot. Earlier generous liquidity in 1999 still formed part of the assessment. At the same time, the switch to a common currency could induce portfolio shifts and breaks in measured money demand. Historical stability in area-wide demand for M3 gave the series weight without resolving those near-term ambiguities. The Governing Council had retained the reference value in December 1999 and intended annual reviews, with the next due in December 2000 (section 2).

The other pillar brought together projections and a broad set of indicators of future prices. The exchange rate mattered through its effect on that outlook. Issing set no exchange-rate objective and promised no automatic response to a currency movement, inflation forecast or monetary aggregate. An investor interpreting a change in the euro would need to establish how much of it might reach prices, under what demand conditions and over what horizon. He presented the monthly press conference, its rapid publication of questions and answers, the Monthly Bulletin and parliamentary appearances as ways to observe that reasoning. His remarks at a market conference explained the strategy and did not announce a rate decision.

The fiscal outlook introduced a second distinction between a cyclical improvement and a durable increase in policy space. The latest estimate put the average euro-area general government deficit at 1.5% of GDP in 1999. Recovery and a falling ratio of interest payments to GDP could take the headline deficit lower even with limited underlying consolidation. Issing read the 2000 projections as implying little consolidation and only a small reduction in debt ratios. High debt and ageing populations could constrain a government’s ability to cut labour taxes or let its budget absorb a future downturn. Improvement in the headline balance alone would give a bondholder insufficient evidence about that flexibility.

For Issing, much of the work of expanding productive capacity belonged to governments and wage setters. Lower non-wage costs for low-paid workers, better incentives to enter work, training for the long-term unemployed and wage structures that accommodated differences in skill and productivity could bring more people into jobs. Reducing barriers to entry, opening network industries, and encouraging productive research investment might also ease constraints on output. Progress in telecommunications, energy, transportation and other networks varied across countries, so any price effects were likely to have different timing and breadth. These were examples of possible reform, not estimates of their separate contributions to growth.

He also warned against mechanically matching wage settlements across members of a common currency. With different productivity levels and local employment conditions, nominal wage convergence could raise unit costs in a weaker region and price unemployed workers out of jobs. Even wage growth matching productivity, while consistent with stable unit labour costs at a broad level, did not by itself guarantee additional hiring. The investment implication was conditional. A recovery sustained by more productive capacity could deliver higher employment and growth with stable prices. The same demand growth meeting persistent skill shortages could change the inflation outlook at a much earlier stage of the recovery than the headline unemployment rate suggested.

questions.question: Were skilled-labour shortages widespread enough to change area-wide wage inflation?
questions.detail: Compare vacancy durations, wage agreements, productivity and unemployment by occupation and region using releases available in January 2000. A limited set of recruitment bottlenecks has different implications for expected short rates from broad wage pressure in excess of productivity.

questions.question: How much of the rapid growth in money reflected liquid portfolios rather than future expenditure?
questions.detail: Consult the ECB’s contemporary monetary statistics and Monthly Bulletin, decomposing M3 by component and counterpart and comparing it with credit and expenditure. Check the timing of portfolio shifts around currency conversion. Persistent credit-backed demand would carry different inflation implications from a one-off switch between assets.

questions.question: What share of the fall in long real rates represented a durable reduction in inflation uncertainty?
questions.detail: Use the November Bulletin study as the starting point. Compare survey expectations, sovereign spreads and instrument liquidity across countries with different initial inflation histories. An investor buying duration on a convergence view needs to know which component of the yield has already fallen and which could reverse.

questions.question: How much fiscal flexibility would remain if the upswing faded?
questions.detail: Use national budget plans and contemporary cyclically adjusted balances to separate policy measures, reduced interest expenditure and temporary revenue growth. Compare debt service and refinancing profiles across member states. This would test whether headline deficit improvement represented usable room to absorb a shock.
